Welcome toOlbers' Dark Sky

Fire lines of sight through a field of stars: how many end on a star, and how bright?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: Olbers' paradox: every line of sight in an infinite, eternal star field ends on a star; a finite age sets a horizon

About this simulation

On screen
The current line of sight seen from the side, from -1 R to 31 R along it and with equal scales across it: the observer O, the blue line growing at 10 R per second, dashed lines at ±R bounding its cylinder, and every star whose centre lies within 2 R of the line, drawn at its distance along the line and its distance from it (only stars within R of the line can block it). The star the line ends on turns light blue. In the finite-age universe a dashed vertical line marks the horizon ct0 and stars beyond it are faint. Above it: a histogram of the lengths of the lines that ended on a star, a plot of the lit fraction of the patch against ct0/ℓ, one dot per completed fill (an infinite-universe fill on the ∞ column), with the law 1 − e−ct0/ℓ and its small-x limit ct0/ℓ (dashed); and a 20 × 20 patch of the observer's sky, one cell per line, pale yellow-white if the line ended on a star and black if not.
Controls
Density n of stars, 30 to 60 per 1000 R3; the universe, infinite and eternal or of finite age; the horizon distance ct0, 0.5 R to 30 R, used only in the finite-age universe. Any change clears the patch. Fire one line grows one line of sight; Fill the patch fires the remaining lines at 20 per second. Click a filled cell to see its line again.
Measured
Lengths are in star radii R. Each line gets its own random star field; its length is the distance to the point where it first enters a star, or to the horizon. The Readouts panel in the sidebar shows the settings, the current line's length L, and for the patch the lit cells and the mean L of the lit lines; the mean free path ℓ = 1/(nπR2) and ct0/ℓ appear once the patch has been filled at the present settings. A lit cell is drawn at one brightness because the surface brightness of a star does not depend on its distance.
Simplifications
Space is static and Euclidean, every star is identical and shines for ever, nothing absorbs light between the stars, and the density is absurdly high so that ℓ is only a few star radii. In the real universe the dark sky comes mainly from the finite age (the horizon); finite stellar lifetimes and the redshift of distant light reduce the brightness further.

Guided Inquiry

1 · An infinite, eternal sky

Set the universe to infinite and eternal and the density n to 30 stars per 1000R3, at which the stars fill only about an eighth of the space. Before filling the patch of sky with 400 lines of sight, predict what the patch looks like.

2 · Doubling the density

Keep the universe infinite and eternal and double the density n to 60 stars per 1000R3. At 30 stars per 1000R3 the mean length of the lines was about 10.6R. Before filling the patch again, predict the mean length now.

3 · Near and far stars

Keep the settings of question 2. Before clicking one lit cell whose line ended within 2R of O and one whose line ended beyond 10R, predict how the brightness of the two cells compares.

4 · A nearby horizon

Set the universe to finite age, the density n to 30 stars per 1000R3 and the horizon distance ct0 to 3R. Before filling the patch, predict how many of the 400 cells light up.

5 · A farther horizon

Keep the finite-age universe and the density at 30 stars per 1000R3, and raise the horizon distance ct0 to 30R, ten times further than in question 4. Before filling the patch, predict the fraction of cells that light up.

6 · The real night sky

Keep the finite-age universe and the density at 30 stars per 1000R3, set the horizon distance ct0 to 1R, about a tenth of ℓ, and fill the patch; about 9 percent of the cells light up, close to ct0/ℓ. In the real universe, with about 108 stars like the Sun in every cubic megaparsec, ℓ is about 1.5 × 1015 times the distance ctH that light travels in the Hubble time tH. Before reading on, predict what fraction of the real sky is covered by stars.

7 · What this shows

In an infinite, eternal universe filled with stars, every line of sight ends on a star, and since surface brightness does not fall with distance the whole sky would blaze like the surface of a star: Olbers' paradox. A finite age sets a horizon ct0; only a fraction 1 − e−ct0/ℓ ≈ ct0/ℓ of the lines reach a star, about 10−15 for the real universe, so the night sky is dark.

Lines of Sight Through a Field of Stars

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Look out at the night sky in any direction. This sim fires lines of sight from an observer O through random fields of stars, and records which lines end on a star and how far they travel. Behind it is an old puzzle, the darkness of the night sky.

What you'll learn

  • How far a line of sight travels before it meets a star.
  • What an infinite, eternal universe and a universe of finite age do to those lines.
  • How much of the sky the stars can cover.
  • Why the real night sky is dark.
Each line of sight from O fills one cell of a 20 × 20 patch of sky: 400 lines, 400 cells.

What's on screen

  • Side view (bottom): the observer O, the blue line of sight growing at 10 R per second, dashed lines at ±R, and grey stars of radius R. The star the line ends on turns light blue.
  • Histogram (top left): the lengths L of the lines that ended on a star.
  • Lit-fraction plot (top middle): the fraction of the patch that lit up against ct0/ℓ, one dot for every completed fill.
  • Patch of sky (top right): one cell per line, pale yellow-white if the line ended on a star, black if not, grey until it is fired.
  • Readouts: the settings, the current length L, the lit cells, ⟨L⟩ on a star, the mean free path ℓ and ct0/ℓ.

03

A line of sight ends on the first star in its cylinder

Each line of sight starts at O and runs in a random direction, drawn along the x axis of the side view. A star of radius R blocks the line when the line passes through it, and that happens when the star's centre lies within R of the line. The line sweeps out a cylinder of radius R (notes, Figure 97b), and the first star whose centre is inside the cylinder ends it.

The side view of one line of sight. Only the star whose centre lies between the dashed lines ±R blocks the line.

The length L of a line is the distance from O to the point where it first enters a star. Each line gets its own random star field, so L differs from line to line. The side view draws stars out to 2R from the line, but only those between the dashed lines can block it.

Key idea. A line of sight ends on the first star whose centre lies within R of the line.
See itFire one line of sight at the opening settings. Watch for: the blue line growing from O at 10 R per second and stopping where it enters a star, which turns light blue. The readout L gives its length in R.
04

The mean length of a line is ℓ = 1/(nπR²)

Take a cylinder of radius R and length ℓ. Its volume is πR²ℓ, so it holds nπR²ℓ star centres on average. Setting that to 1 gives the mean distance a line travels before it meets a star, the mean free path (notes, eq. 9.10):

Equation (9.10). n is the number of stars per unit volume and R their radius.

This is the argument for a molecule's mean free path, with πR² as the cross-section. There is no factor √2, because the stars move so much more slowly than light that they can be treated as at rest.

The sim's density is per 1000 R³, so ℓ = 1000/(π × density) in units of R. At the opening density 30, ℓ = 10.61 R. At 60, ℓ = 5.31 R. Doubling n halves ℓ. It does not shrink by 21/3, the factor for the spacing between neighbouring stars, because the cylinder's cross-section stays fixed. Over a filled patch, the mean L of the lit lines typically lands within about 10 percent of ℓ.

Key idea. The mean length is ℓ = 1/(nπR²): twice the density, half the length.
See itFill the patch at n = 30, then double n to 60 and fill again. Watch for: ⟨L⟩ on a star falling from about 10.6 R to about 5.3 R.
05

In an infinite universe every line ends on a star

The chance that a line travels a distance D without meeting a star follows from the mean length. In a further distance dD it meets one with probability dD/ℓ, so the survival probability P falls by dP = −P dD/ℓ. With P(0) = 1 this gives P = e−D/ℓ (notes).

In an infinite, eternal universe D has no limit. P goes to 0, and every line of sight ends on a star, however sparse the stars are.

At n = 30 the stars fill only 12.6 percent of the volume, 4πR³n/3, yet about 37 percent of the lines are longer than ℓ = 10.6 R and about 6 percent run past 30 R. That is about 24 lines in the dashed ≥30 R bar of the histogram. None escape: all 400 cells light up.

Key idea. With no limit on D, every line of sight ends on a star.
See itFill the patch at n = 30 in the infinite and eternal universe. Watch for: every cell lit, with the lit readout at 400 of 400 (100.0%), and about two dozen lines in the ≥30 R bar.
06

Surface brightness does not fall with distance, so every cell is equally bright

Add up the starlight without any hiding. A thin shell of radius r and thickness dr holds 4πr²n dr stars, and each delivers a flux L/4πr² (notes, eq. 9.9):

Equation (9.9). The flux of a shell does not depend on r, so stars out to a distance D give nLD, which grows without limit.
The outer shell holds more stars, but each is fainter by just the right factor.

Hiding by nearer stars cuts the sum down, but the sky stays bright, since every line ends on a star. A distant star's flux is smaller by 1/r², and it also covers a solid angle smaller by the same factor, so its surface brightness is the same as a near star's. The specific intensity does not change along a ray in empty space (notes, Section 3.3).

So every direction would be as bright as the surface of a star, and the Earth would be heated to nearly the temperature of the solar surface. This is Olbers' paradox. The sim draws every lit cell in one colour for this reason.

Key idea. A lit cell is as bright as a stellar surface, whether its star is near or far.
See itFill the patch at n = 30, then look at a cell with a short line and one with a long line. Watch for: the two cells the same pale yellow-white, though the blue line ends close to O for the first and far from O for the second.
07

A finite age puts a horizon on the sky

Light that reaches us now left its source less than the age of the universe ago. So we receive light only from stars nearer than about ct0 (the expansion changes this by a factor of order one, which does not matter here). In the sim this is the horizon, a dashed vertical line, with the stars beyond it faint. A line that reaches ct0 without meeting a star ends black. The fraction of lines that meet a star in time is (notes, eq. 9.11):

Equation (9.11). The approximation holds only for ct0 much smaller than ℓ.
The law at n = 30, where ℓ = 10.61 R, with the horizons used below.

At ct0 = 3 R, 1 − e−0.283 = 0.246, about 98 of 400 cells. The small-x value 0.283 is already 15 percent too high. At 30 R the fraction is 0.941, about 376 cells: ten times the horizon, only 3.8 times the cells. A 400-cell patch scatters around these, typically 86 to 113 and 369 to 384 cells.

Key idea. A horizon at ct0 lights the fraction 1 − e−ct₀/ℓ, which cannot exceed 1.
See itSet the finite-age universe at n = 30 with ct0 = 3 R, and fill the patch. Watch for: the lit readout near 25 percent, about 100 of 400 cells, and ct0/ℓ = 0.283.
See itRaise ct0 to 30 R at n = 30 and fill again. Watch for: the lit readout near 94 percent, about 376 of 400 cells, with a few cells still black.
08

The real night sky is dark because ct₀ is far smaller than ℓ

The mean density of starlight in the universe corresponds to roughly 108 stars like the Sun in every cubic megaparsec. With it, ℓ is of order 1015 times ctH, the distance light travels in the Hubble time (notes). The inquiry uses 1.5 × 1015. Then only about ctH/ℓ ≈ 7 × 10−16 of the lines of sight reach a star: about one part in 1015 of the sky.

The sky could not fill with starlight even if the universe were older. The stars would have to shine for a time ℓ/c, of order 1025 years, while a star like the Sun shines for about 1010 years (notes, Problem 5). The redshift of distant light darkens the sky further.

The sim cannot reach 10−15. Its density is absurdly high, so ℓ is only a few R, and its smallest horizon, 0.5 R, gives ct0/ℓ = 0.047.

Key idea. The night is dark because the universe is too young for more than a tiny fraction of the lines of sight to reach a star.
See itSet ct0 = 1 R, about a tenth of ℓ, at n = 30 and fill the patch. Watch for: about 9 percent of the cells lit, roughly 36 of 400, close to ct0/ℓ = 0.094, with every line shorter than the 1 R horizon.
09

Summary

In one line. A line of sight ends on the first star in its path, and how much of the sky those stars cover depends on the star density, the age of the universe and the mean length ℓ of a line.
  • ℓ = 1/(nπR²) is the mean distance to the first star; doubling n halves it.
  • Infinite and eternal: P = e−D/ℓ goes to 0, every line ends on a star, and every lit cell is as bright as a stellar surface. That is Olbers' paradox.
  • Finite age: the fraction lit is 1 − e−ct₀/ℓ, close to ct0/ℓ only when ct0 ≪ ℓ.
  • Real universe: ctH/ℓ is about 10−15, so almost every line of sight is still dark.

Common mix-ups

  • "Far stars are too faint to count." They are smaller in the same proportion, so surface brightness is unchanged.
  • "A horizon nearer than ℓ lights nothing." A fraction 1 − e−ct₀/ℓ still meets a star: a quarter at 3 R.
  • "Ten times the horizon lights ten times the sky." The fraction cannot exceed 1: from 3 R to 30 R it goes from 0.25 to 0.94.
  • "The stars beyond the horizon are missing." They are there. Their light has not had time to arrive.

Things to try on your own

  • At n = 30, find the ct0 that lights about half the cells.
  • At n = 60, repeat the 3 R horizon and compare its lit fraction with the n = 30 one.
